title: From Kharkiv Noodles to a Dry Island off Nha Trang
dek: Pham Nhat Vuong built an instant-noodle business in crisis-hit Ukraine, then in 2000 began moving its profits into a barren island at home.

story.event: Moving instant-noodle profits from Ukraine into a resort on Hon Tre island
story.industry: food (instant noodles), then property and hotels
story.summary: Pham Nhat Vuong started a business in Kharkiv, Ukraine, in 1993 with borrowed money, first a restaurant and then instant noodles sold as Mivina from 1995, which became Ukraine's dominant noodle brand. In 2000, while still running the Ukrainian company Technocom, he set up Vinpearl and began building a resort on the barren island of Hon Tre off Nha Trang, followed by the Vincom tower in Hanoi. Around 2010 he sold Technocom to Nestle for a reported $150 million; his Vietnamese companies merged as Vingroup in 2012.
paragraphs: On 8 August 1993, the date Vingroup still counts as its founding, Pham Nhat Vuong and three younger colleagues began a business in Kharkiv, Ukraine. Vuong had studied geology in Moscow on a scholarship, and a clothing trade there had failed and left him in debt. With a few thousand dollars borrowed from friends, he and his wife opened a restaurant in an old factory canteen.

Ukraine was in economic crisis, with empty shops and many goods rationed by coupon. Vuong saw demand for cheap, quick food and began making instant noodles with about 30 workers. The brand, Mivina, from the Vietnamese for Vietnamese noodles, launched in 1995 and spread across the country. His company, Technocom, added instant potatoes, seasoning and packaging; in 2003 the Kyiv Post put its output at 70,000 tonnes a year. Vuong has said his dream at the time was not a large one: he wanted to lift his family out of poverty. VietNamNet later reported that around 1997 he had meant to stop once he had made $2 million.

He did not stop, and he did not stay. In 2000, still running the Ukrainian business, he began putting its profits into Vietnam. He set up Vinpearl and chose Hon Tre, a dry island off Nha Trang with no fresh water, for a resort. One newspaper headline at the time said the money had been thrown into the sea. Before building, he studied hotels in Phuket and shopping centres in Singapore. The resort opened with 225 rooms, and the following year came Vincom in Hanoi, the city's first commercial tower complex.

For about a decade the two lives ran side by side. Around 2010 Technocom and Mivina were sold to Nestle, for a reported $150 million. In 2012 Vuong's Vietnamese companies merged as Vingroup, and in 2013 Forbes listed him as Vietnam's first dollar billionaire. Speaking in 2019, he described how his reasons had changed: at first he wanted to earn enough to spare his parents hardship, then the work became a passion, and in the end he hoped to do something worthwhile for others.

quote.text: Wherever the peasant tills the hard earth, there does thy joy gush out in the green of the corn, wherever man displaces the entangled forest, smooths the stony ground, and clears for himself a homestead, there does thy joy enfold it in orderliness and peace.
quote.source_title: Sadhana: The Realisation of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #6842
quote.connection: Tagore finds joy inside work rather than apart from it, in corn grown on hard earth and a homestead cleared from stony ground. Vuong took profits made far from home and spent them on a dry island most people thought a waste, and he describes his reasons growing as the work did.

reflection: A change of direction is often pictured as one brave leap. Vuong's was slower. For about ten years the noodle business kept running while the island was built, and it was sold only after the resort and the Hanoi tower were open.

His reasons changed too. He began wanting to keep his parents out of hardship, and later spoke of passion and then of doing something useful for others. If your own reasons for this work have shifted since you started, it does not mean you have lost the thread. It may simply be how the thread grows.
invitation: Write one sentence on why you keep doing your work today, without looking back at why you began. Put it somewhere you will see it again next week.

cross_checks.claim: Vuong's noodle business began in Kharkiv in 1993.
He first opened a restaurant in Kharkiv with money borrowed from friends.
In 2000, while still running the Ukrainian business, he set up Vinpearl and began investing in Hon Tre island.
Technocom was sold to Nestle around 2010 for a reported $150 million.
Forbes listed him as Vietnam's first dollar billionaire in 2013.

research_notes: Dates: Vingroup counts 8 August 1993 as its founding (VietnamFinance, VietNamNet 2015) and the Kyiv Post (2003) says Mivina products were made from 1993, while Inventure (from Ekonomichna Pravda) dates Technocom to 1995; VietNamNet and VietnamFinance date the Mivina brand to 1995. The story uses 1993 for the start of the business and 1995 for the brand. Sale: 2010 for about $150 million in Inventure, VietNamNet (2013, 2015) and VietTimes; VietnamFinance says the brand was transferred in 2009 without naming the buyer; the story says 'around 2010' and 'a reported $150 million'. Nestle's own press release was blocked to automated requests. Borrowed start-up money: 'a few thousand dollars' from friends (Bao Phap Luat, VietTimes) versus about $10,000 borrowed by his family (Inventure); VietTimes adds $100,000 borrowed from friends at up to 8% a month for Technocom; the story says 'a few thousand dollars' for the restaurant only. Workforce: about 30 at the start (Bao Phap Luat, VietNamNet English 2019) and later 3,000 (Bao Phap Luat, VietTimes) or about 1,900 (VietNamNet 2015); the story uses only the starting figure. Market share: VietTimes says 97% of Ukraine's instant-noodle market by 2004, VietNamNet 2015 says 97% of consumers used it; not used. The restaurant's name (Thang Long in VietTimes; Bao Phap Luat says the Thang Long restaurant came later) is left out. The $2 million retirement plan is VietNamNet's reported speech, attributed as such. Vuong gives few interviews; his statements about his early dream and his changing motives are taken from Vietnamese-language reporting (VietTimes) and are paraphrased in English rather than quoted, since any quotation would be a translation. Country and region: the business base was Kharkiv, Ukraine, but the change of direction itself, the island and the resort, happened in Vietnam, so country is Vietnam and region Southeast Asia. Tagore's passage is a prayer about joy in work; it is applied by analogy.
